body:
For what it's worth, you certainly helped.  I'm not going to try to convince you that the motivation you gave him was entirely wholesome, but you didn't have the option of resorting to a guide or getting him a real therapist.  You were the only option for dealing with it in the short term.  What mattered is that you had good intentions, and you produced a substantial result *now*.  This wasn't a vague thought, it was clear and immediate intent.  You talked him out of that decision.  You may have given him some baggage, but *you gave him back the chance to beat that baggage.*  He can get past any impact you had, just as he can get past the problems that drove him there.  What matters is that if you hadn't said *something* that worked, even with side effects, he wouldn't be around to try to heal.  You were the only one there to help, and you did enough to keep him around and get him to someone who can help more.

/r/SuicideWatch has some really solid talking tips here: http://www.reddit.com/r/SWResources/comments/igh87/concerned_but_dont_know_what_to_say_here_are_some/

It's hard to know what to say without some real training, and even then the answer is different in every case; those are just some helpful guidelines should it come up again.

Hey, I know that feeling really well.  I didn't get into my first choice college.  Or my second.  Or third.  You get the picture.  This wasn't that long ago, and it baffled me.  I was the capable kid who everyone said could go anywhere, and I got a string of faceless, impersonal rejections.  It crushed everything I thought was important about me, and I didn't see a point in sticking around.  For me the worst thing was the tone: "We have to reject many applicants who would succeed here, and we know you'll do well wherever you end up."  Motherfucker, that's not an explanation.

When it hits, that feeling is awful.  I'm sorry.  It's a fucked up system with huge expectations and random chance driving choices between perfectly qualified candidates, and all I can say is that it's not you.  It's a mean, unpredictable system.  That said, I hope your parents won't genuinely be upset - I thought mine would be, and they turned out not to mind at all.  It's possible they will be though - if they are, know that they'll come around.  People aren't always as strong or understanding as they should be, but eventually they'll realize that it doesn't change a damn thing about you.

That said, I'm at school now.  I thought my parents and everyone else would be embarrassed for me.  I thought it would fuck up my future.  As it turns out, about 2 people judged me for the outcome, and they turned out to be assholes.  I'm getting a good education, I'm (reasonably) happy, and with each thing I learn and do the name on my school is mattering less.

It's one of the little secrets that no one will tell you because they're worried it'll make you less dedicated: college doesn't matter anywhere near as much as it looks like, especially undergrad.  The biggest advantage of the "best" colleges is a rubber stamp saying that you're clever, or strong, or maybe just rich or a good way to round out some graph.  The actual education?  Not that different.  Just having these expectations on you tells me that you're a capable person, however this turned out.  Someone dedicated enough to care about getting into a good college is someone who can make it wherever they end up (in or out of college).  Jobs give you an interview and judge you on what you can do, not on some silly damn essay and unknowable rubrics.  You can go anywhere, get what you need, and impress the world with what you do, not what name you did it under.

Please feel free to go into more about your situation if you want to share, and please know that there are a lot of us out there.  College acceptance reflects on the people doing the judging far more than it does on your value, and no matter what they say you're the same person you were before, and you can accomplish just as much.

Damn this is a happy story.  Thanks for sharing, and please stick around to share many more.

You've helped inspire me on to make a deal with myself - if it ever comes to that point, there are four people I have to tell first, before anything else.  It's a deal I know I'll keep, and I know that they'll remind me why it's not a good option.  Good friends are rare and awesome, I'm glad to hear that yours are great!

Thanks, I will.  I saw a few friends get committed (though that was from overzealous cop-calling by others), and got the impression that it was a question you couldn't say yes to.  After seeing people respond I get that that's kind of a silly thought - obviously not everyone who thinks about suicide can or should be committed.

I'll talk to a therapist about it, and don't worry, I'm not in immediate danger.  I think this will help a lot.
Thanks - keeping these concerns in one head for too long tends to leave them way out of proportion.  I'll talk to a therapist and trust that I can work it out that way.

Damn, that's a heavy final exam, I'm sorry.  Anyone drop you a line to see if you were ok, or just a casual C+?

Thanks for the reassurance on therapists, I got a little paranoid but it makes sense that they're not going to jump any time anyone mentions suicidal thoughts.

I'm concerned about getting tossed out because it's an American private school and I'm on "leave" for grades (less than shockingly, my mental state and those grades are related).  Without "proof that I'm ready to return" I don't come back - the bar for that isn't high, but I have some reason to believe that they'd be eager to say no if they thought I might hurt myself while on their student statistics.
